title_original: Steven Paul Talks Up Federal Film & TV Tax Credit: “It’s Going To Be Good For The World” – Industry Days Doha

blocks.text: Hollywood veteran Steven Paul carried a flag for the push for a Hollywood film and TV incentive to Qatar on Friday.

Speaking in a fireside chat at the Qatar Film Committee ’s Industry Days event in Doha, Paul said the proposed tax credit, covering between 20 to 30% of the U.S. spend, would be good for the world, without explaining the reasoning behind this declaration.

“I’ve got two tiers to discuss, regarding why it’ll be good for the world, but right away, it’s going to be good for the entertainment business because a lot more money comes into the business, which makes it more healthy,” he said.

blocks.text: “You’re going to have banks, hedge funds, everybody looking at it as a more profitable business, and when they see profits or everybody talking profits, profits, all of a sudden more money comes into the business… there’ll be a huge amount that comes in, and there’ll be a lot more independent films made.”

Reiterating points made in a recent panel on the proposed incentive at the AFM earlier this month , Paul said the new federal incentive could be combined with state tax incentives, meaning productions could be in a position to cover up to 50 to 60% of the budget.

links.text: in a recent panel on the proposed incentive at the AFM earlier this month

blocks.text: “Where they couldn’t make it before, independents getting 50, 60% of their budget already done, they’re going to find a way, where there’s a deferment or they’ll get their mother and father to put something on. All of a sudden, boom! They’re going to be making a lot more productions than they had before.”

Paul’s comments coincided with fresh push on Friday to get the federal film and TV tax credit bill over the line in Congress by the end of this year, as 60 house members and four senators signed up for the bipartisan legislation.

links.text: coincided with fresh push on Friday

blocks.text: A report commissioned by Hollywood unions published in October, found that between 1999 and 2024, the share of production spending by major U.S. studios on movies filmed either partially or primarily within the country declined from 74% to 42%, while the share of TV production spending is down from 94% to 64%.

links.text: A report commissioned by Hollywood unions

blocks.text: Paul, who produces under his SP Media banner, is among those who have sought more financially favorable environments, recently shooting his production Nixon’s Gamble in the UK.

Set in 1948, the film follows ambitious, 35-year-old Congressman Richard Nixon as he stakes his career on proving that Alger Hiss, one of Washington’s most respected diplomats, is secretly working for the Soviet Union.

“There is pictures that just should be made in America that are not being made in America… Why am I filming a film about Richard Nixon, when he was 35 years old in 1948, in London… when it’s about Washington D.C. That should be filmed in America,” he said.
“So there’s just films that need to be done there… and I think with these with these tax credits, it’ll be comparable,” he said.
